name: Bikaneri bhujia
summary: Thin, crisp strands of moth-bean and gram-flour dough, spiced with pepper and chilli and deep-fried. Bikaner's best-known snack, made largely as a cottage industry.

history.text: The first batch is commonly dated to 1877, in the princely state of Bikaner during the reign of Maharaja Dungar Singh.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Bikaneri Bhujia is a registered Geographical Indication of Rajasthan. A news report from September 2010 lists it among twelve newly registered products.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

current_form_note: Classic Bikaneri bhujia: moth bean and gram flour with chilli and pepper.

name: Dal baati churma
summary: Hard wheat-dough balls baked over coals and soaked in ghee, eaten with spiced lentils and churma, a sweet of crushed wheat, ghee and jaggery or sugar.

history.text: Accounts link baati to the time of Bappa Rawal, founder of the Mewar kingdom, and describe it as a wartime meal of his clan.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: A popular story says soldiers buried dough in the desert sand and let the sun bake it. Our source calls this anecdotal.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Two folk stories explain churma: a cook spilling cane juice on baati, or home cooks soaking baati in sweet syrup. There is no firm evidence for either.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

name: Ghewar
summary: A lacy, honeycombed disc of fried flour-and-ghee batter soaked in sugar syrup, often topped with rabri and nuts. Rajasthan's sweet for Teej and the monsoon month of Shravan.

history.text: Ghewar is said to have been made first by cooks in Rajasthan's royal kitchens before it reached ordinary homes. No dates are given for this.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Mirabai, the 16th-century poet-saint, describes offering ghevar to Krishna in one of her poems.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: The name may come from the Sanskrit ghṛtapūra, roughly 'ghee cake'.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Laxmi Mishthan Bhandar in Jaipur introduced a chhena (fresh cheese) version in 1961.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Dhokla
summary: A soft, tangy steamed cake of fermented rice and gram-flour batter, cut into squares and finished with mustard seeds. Gujarat eats it for breakfast, with tea and at weddings.

history.text: Popular accounts say an 11th-century Jain text mentions dukkia, a steamed dish of pulses, and call it dhokla's ancestor. They give different years (1066 or 1068 CE) and don't name the text, so we can't confirm it yet.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: The word dhokla appears in Varnaka Samuccaya, a Gujarati text dated to around 1520 CE. It is the earliest written use of the name we know of.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: K. T. Achaya records the classic method: two parts rice to one part gram flour, soured overnight with curd, steamed in a tray, then cut and finished with fried mustard seeds, fresh coriander and grated coconut.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Who first made khaman, the all-gram-flour cousin raised with soda instead of a long ferment, is not recorded in the sources we checked.
history.label: UNKNOWN

current_form_note: Classic dhokla as Achaya describes it. Khaman is often tempered with green chilli.

name: Khandvi
summary: Thin sheets of gram flour cooked with yogurt, spread out to set, then rolled into soft spirals and dressed with a tempering. Also called patuli or dahivadi.

history.text: We found no dated history for khandvi in our sources; they record only its other names, patuli, dahivadi and suralichi vadi.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Undhiyu
summary: A winter casserole from Surat of beans, small aubergines, potatoes, yam, unripe banana and fenugreek dumplings, slow-cooked with a green paste of coriander, ginger, garlic and chilli.

history.text: The name comes from the Gujarati undhu, 'upside down', because it was traditionally cooked in earthen pots (matlu) turned upside down and buried in a fire pit.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Our source gives no date for when undhiyu began.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Puran poli
summary: A soft flatbread stuffed with cooked chana dal sweetened with jaggery and scented with cardamom or nutmeg, eaten warm with ghee at festivals across Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra.

history.text: The Manasollasa, a 12th-century Sanskrit encyclopedia written for King Someshvara III in Karnataka, refers to the dish.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Ayurvedic works such as the Bhavaprakasha also give a recipe for it.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Misal pav
summary: A fiery curry of sprouted moth beans (usal) with a thin spicy gravy, topped with farsan, onion and lemon, eaten with soft bread rolls. Every Maharashtra city argues its version is best.

history.text: Our sources give no date or founding story for misal. They name Mamledar, Bedekar and Katakir among shops that have served it for decades.
history.label: UNKNOWN

history.text: In 2015 the misal at Aaswad in Dadar, Mumbai, was named the world's tastiest vegetarian dish at the FoodieHub Awards in London.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Vada pav
summary: A spiced potato fritter in gram-flour batter, tucked into a soft bread roll with fiery garlic chutney and fried green chilli. Mumbai's cheap, fast lunch.

history.text: Vada pav is commonly credited to Ashok Vaidya and Sudhakar Mhatre, who are said to have created it in Mumbai in 1966.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

name: Khatkhate
summary: A thick Goan Hindu stew of at least five vegetables, such as radish, sweet potato, corn and pumpkin, cooked with coconut, jaggery, kokum, tamarind and tirphal.

history.text: It is commonly served at Goan Hindu weddings, religious ceremonies and festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Our source gives no date for when the dish began.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Goan khaje
summary: Crunchy sticks of fried gram-flour dough coated in jaggery, piled into mountains at temple zatras and church feasts across Goa.

history.text: Khaje is sold at the fairs held after temple zatras and church feasts.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: The All Goa Khaje Producers Association applied for a GI in July 2019. A Goan paper reported the registration in July 2020; the national GI list shows the year as 2021–22.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Bebinca
summary: A Goan layer cake of egg yolk, coconut milk, sugar, flour and ghee, baked one thin layer at a time, traditionally seven to sixteen layers. A Christmas favourite.

history.text: Bebinca belongs to Indo-Portuguese cooking in Goa and is especially popular at Christmas.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Our source gives no date or founding story. A widely repeated tale about a nun named Bebiana does not appear in it, so we don't repeat it as fact.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Sarson da saag and makki di roti

local_names.text: ਸਰ੍ਹੋਂ ਦਾ ਸਾਗ ਤੇ ਮੱਕੀ ਦੀ ਰੋਟੀ
local_names.translit: sarhon da saag te makki di roti

summary: Slow-cooked mustard greens with garlic, ginger and chilli, finished with ghee or butter, eaten with flatbread made from maize flour. Punjab's winter meal.

history.text: Sarson comes from the Sanskrit sarṣapa, 'mustard', and saag from śāka, 'greens'.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: One source cited in our reference says mustard has been grown in Punjab for millennia; the maize in makki di roti, by contrast, is an American crop.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

current_form_note: The pairing with makki di roti can't be older than maize in India.

name: Amritsari kulcha
summary: A crisp, layered tandoor bread stuffed with spiced mashed potato, brushed with butter and usually eaten with chole. Amritsar's breakfast.

history.text: It is said to have originated in Amritsar, inspired by the Peshawari khameeri roti, a sourdough flatbread. No date is given.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: The word kulcha comes from Persian, for a disc-shaped leavened loaf.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Kashmiri dum aloo
summary: Small potatoes, skinned and fried, then slow-cooked in a yogurt sauce with fennel, ginger and red chilli. Part of Kashmiri Pandit cooking.

history.text: Dum aloo is part of traditional Kashmiri Pandit cuisine; dum means slow cooking in steam.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Nadru yakhni
summary: Slices of lotus stem simmered in a creamy, gently spiced yogurt gravy. A slow, elaborate curry from the Kashmir Valley.

history.text: A story says lotus stem entered Kashmiri food in the 15th century, when boatmen of the ruler Zain-ul-Abidin picked lotus roots on the Gill Sar lake for his supper.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

name: Siddu
summary: A steamed bun of yeasted wheat dough stuffed with a savoury paste of lentils, poppy seeds and walnuts, or a sweet filling, and eaten hot with ghee.

history.text: Siddu is said to come from the Mahasu area (now in the former Shimla district) and to have spread to Kullu, Mandi and Sirmaur. It was traditionally made by shepherds.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

name: Kangri dham
summary: A festive meal of the Kangra valley served in courses: rice, madra (chickpeas in yogurt), black lentils, a sweet-sour pumpkin khatta and sweet rice. No onion or garlic.

history.text: Dham is cooked by hereditary cooks called botis for temple festivals, weddings and religious ceremonies, and is strictly satvik, with no onion or garlic.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Our source gives no date for when the tradition began.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Kafuli
summary: A thick green curry of spinach and fenugreek leaves, thickened with rice flour and tempered with garlic and ginger in mustard oil. Garhwal also calls it dhapdi.

history.text: It is traditionally cooked in an iron pan over a wood fire and eaten with rice or finger-millet (mandua) roti.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Our source makes no claim about when kafuli began.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Bal mithai
summary: Dark, fudge-like cubes of roasted khoya coated with tiny white sugar balls. Almora's famous sweet, nicknamed 'chocolate' for its colour.

history.text: Joga Lal Sah, a sweet-maker in business in Almora's Lal Bazaar since 1865, is credited with creating bal mithai as it is known today; his descendants still run the shop.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: A local story says soldiers from Kumaon carried bal mithai while serving in Burma in the Second World War.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

name: Agra petha
summary: Translucent candied pieces of ash gourd, soaked in lime water to stay firm, then boiled in sugar syrup. Agra's counters sell it in many flavours.

history.text: A legend says petha was invented in Shah Jahan's kitchens to feed the Taj Mahal's workers. Our source calls this highly unlikely: petha is not in Shah Jahan's cookbook, the Nuskha-e-Shahjahani.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Its real date of invention is unknown. Similar sweets are recorded before the Mughals.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Banarasi tirangi barfi
summary: A tricoloured barfi in saffron, white and green, the colours of the Indian flag, made in Varanasi.

history.text: Press reports describe it as a sweet sold by supporters of the freedom struggle during the Quit India Movement.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Banaras Tirangi Barfi received a Geographical Indication in April 2024.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Bedmi puri
summary: A thick, crisp fried bread whose dough and stuffing both use spiced urad dal, eaten hot with a potato and tomato curry. A North Indian breakfast.

history.text: Where bedmi began is argued over: Delhi or Uttar Pradesh.
history.label: DISPUTED

sides.text: Many treat it as a classic Delhi Sunday breakfast.
Others place it in UP; one writer suggests it grew out of Varanasi's stuffed kachori tradition and travelled to Delhi.

name: Indori poha-jalebi
summary: Steamed flattened rice with peanuts, mustard and curry leaves, topped with onion, Ratlami sev and jeeravan masala, eaten with hot jalebi. Indore's morning ritual.

history.text: Indori poha is believed to have been created in Indore after independence in 1947. No people are named.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: The oldest known recipe for jalebi-like fritters is in a 10th-century Arabic cookbook by Ibn Sayyar al-Warraq.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: In India, a Jain work by Jinasura of about 1450 mentions jalebi at a merchant's dinner.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Dal bafla
summary: Wheat dough balls boiled and then baked, softer than Rajasthani baati, dunked in ghee and eaten with spiced dal. A Malwa favourite.

history.text: Our source calls dal bafla native to Malwa in Madhya Pradesh, while noting that parts of Rajasthan also claim it.
history.label: DISPUTED

sides.text: Parts of Rajasthan claim it too.

name: Mysore pak
summary: A rich, porous sweet of gram flour cooked with sugar syrup and a generous amount of ghee, set and cut into blocks. Often scented with cardamom.

history.text: Tradition says a palace cook named Kakasura Madappa created it in Mysore Palace during the reign of Krishna Raja Wadiyar IV and named it after the city.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

name: Bisi bele bath
summary: Rice and toor dal cooked together with vegetables, tamarind and a special spice blend, finished with ghee. The name means 'hot lentil rice'.

history.text: It is said to have begun in the Mysore Palace kitchens, where its recipe stayed close to secret among palace cooks for a long time. No dates are given.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

name: Dharwad peda
summary: A brown, crumbly milk sweet made by cooking milk with sugar for a long time until it caramelises, traditionally from the milk of Dharwadi buffaloes.

history.text: Family history says the Thakurs moved from Unnao in Uttar Pradesh after a plague in the late 18th century. Ram Ratan Singh Thakur began selling pedas, and his grandson Babu Singh Thakur made the Line Bazaar shop famous.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Dharwad Pedha is a registered Geographical Indication of Karnataka.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Avial
summary: A thick mix of many vegetables, such as yam, plantain, ash gourd, drumstick and beans, cooked with ground coconut and curd and finished with coconut oil and curry leaves. A fixture of the sadhya feast.

history.text: A legend credits Bhima of the Mahabharata: working as a cook in King Virata's kitchen, he chopped every vegetable he had, boiled them together and topped them with coconut.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Another story says a Travancore king, short of curry at a feast, had his cook use the leftover vegetables; the dish was then served at the sadhya.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

name: Puttu and kadala curry
summary: Cylinders of steamed coarse rice flour layered with grated coconut, eaten with a spicy curry of black chickpeas. Kerala's classic breakfast.

history.text: In Tamil Nadu, a myth about a flood of the Vaigai river and the Pandya king Arimarthana involves puttu; it is re-enacted every year at the Avani Mula festival at the Meenakshi temple in Madurai.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Our source gives no date for when puttu began.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Appam with vegetable stew

diet.nonveg_variants_note: Often served with egg, chicken or mutton stew instead.

summary: Bowl-shaped pancakes of fermented rice batter and coconut milk, soft in the middle and lacy at the edges, served with a mild coconut-milk vegetable stew.

history.text: Food historian K. T. Achaya, as cited by journalist Vir Sanghvi, says Tamil Sangam poems describe appams sold with modakam in the street markets of Madurai.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: A 2018 study of Chola-era temple inscriptions reports an early appam recipe carved on the walls of the Srirangam temple as an offering.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: The name may come from the Sanskrit apupa, a kind of fried sweet.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

name: Idli
summary: Soft, steamed cakes of fermented rice and black-gram batter, eaten with sambar and coconut chutney across South India.

history.text: The Kannada work Vaddaradhane (920 CE) mentions iddalige, made from black gram alone, with no rice.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: The Sanskrit Manasollasa (1130 CE) describes iddarika. These early recipes lack rice, long fermentation and steaming; recipes like today's idli appear only after about 1250 CE.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Where the steamed, fermented idli came from is disputed.
history.label: DISPUTED

sides.text: K. T. Achaya speculated that cooks in Indianised kingdoms of Indonesia invented the steamed idli and brought it to India between 800 and 1200 CE, citing a dish called 'kedli'. Others could not find a recipe by that name.
Colleen Taylor Sen argues fermentation was discovered independently in India, and archaeologist Dorian Fuller says steaming was used in Neolithic South India around 2000 BCE.

name: Ven pongal
summary: A soft, savoury porridge of rice and moong dal cooked with ghee, black pepper, cumin, ginger and curry leaves, often topped with fried cashews. 'Ven' means white.

history.text: Our source gives no history for ven pongal; it only explains that 'venn' means white, citing Winslow's Tamil dictionary of 1862.
history.label: UNKNOWN

current_form_note: The cashew garnish is optional; it would date the dish to after the 1560s.

name: Srivilliputtur palkova
summary: A creamy, fudge-like sweet of rich milk slowly reduced with sugar, made in the temple town of Srivilliputhur from local high-fat milk.

history.text: A press report traces the town's palkova to about 1921, when Dev Singh opened Lala Sweets near the Andal temple, inspired by the temple's milk prasadam.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Srivilliputtur Palkova is a registered Geographical Indication of Tamil Nadu; the local milk producers' cooperative led the application.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Kovilpatti kadalai mittai
summary: A crunchy peanut brittle bound with jaggery syrup, made in Kovilpatti and cut into bars.

history.text: It received a Geographical Indication in April 2020 after a five-year wait.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: The makers' application says its taste comes from local groundnuts, chosen jaggery and water from the Thamirabarani river, cooked over firewood.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Our sources give no founding date or founder.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Pesarattu
summary: A thin, crisp crepe of ground whole green gram with green chilli and ginger, often stuffed with upma. Eaten with ginger chutney.

history.text: Pesarattu comes from coastal Andhra Pradesh; its Telugu name means 'green gram pancake'.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Our source gives no date for when it began.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Bandar laddu
summary: A soft, crumbly laddu of gram flour, jaggery syrup and ghee from Machilipatnam (Bandar), also called thokkudu laddu.

history.text: The GI Registry registered Bandar Laddu as a foodstuff on 3 May 2017.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Our sources give no origin story or early date.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Rasagola / rosogolla
summary: Balls of fresh chhena cheese simmered in light sugar syrup until spongy. Both Odisha and West Bengal claim it, and each holds its own GI for its version.

history.text: Where rasagola began is disputed between Odisha and West Bengal.
history.label: DISPUTED

sides.text: Odia accounts trace it to Puri: Lakshmi is offered rasagola in the Niladri Bije ritual of the Jagannath temple, and Odia historians date this offering to the 12th century. A 15th-century Odia Ramayana by Balaram Das is cited for the word 'rasagola'.
Bengal credits the spongy version to Kolkata confectioner Nobin Chandra Das in 1868. Others name Braja Moira (1866) or Haradhan Moira of Phulia.

history.text: Historians K. T. Achaya and Chitra Banerji found no reference to cheese, including chhena, in India before the 17th century, which makes a 12th-century chhena offering hard to accept.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: West Bengal received a GI for 'Banglar Rasogolla' on 14 November 2017, and Odisha one for 'Odisha Rasagola' on 29 July 2019. The tags cover each state's version, not the question of origin.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Chhena poda
summary: Fresh chhena kneaded with sugar and semolina, then baked for hours until the outside caramelises. The name means 'burnt cheese' in Odia.

history.text: It is credited to Sudarsan Sahu, who experimented with leftover cheese at his hotel in Dashapalla, Odisha, after 1947.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Chhenapoda Dibasa, a day celebrating the sweet, has been observed since 11 April 2022, his birth anniversary.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Dalma
summary: Toor dal cooked with chopped vegetables such as raw papaya, plantain, aubergine and pumpkin, and finished with panch phutana, a five-seed tempering.

history.text: Our source describes dalma but gives no history. Links often made between dalma and the Jagannath temple kitchen still need a source.
history.label: UNKNOWN

current_form_note: Vegetables vary; papaya and pumpkin are optional and do not set the age limit.

name: Mishti doi
summary: Thickened milk sweetened with sugar or date-palm jaggery and set overnight into a caramel-coloured yogurt, traditionally in porous earthen pots.

history.text: It is traditionally set in earthenware, whose porous walls let water escape, thickening the yogurt.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Our source gives no date for its origin; it names Nabadwip, Kolkata and Bogra (Bangladesh) as famous centres.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Burdwan mihidana
summary: Tiny, saffron-coloured fried grains of fine rice flour and a little gram flour, soaked in syrup. A finer cousin of boondi.

history.text: Two accounts disagree on who created mihidana and when.
history.label: DISPUTED

sides.text: Sweet-maker Vairabchandra Nag is credited with creating it for the lunch given to Lord Curzon when he visited Bardhaman on 19 August 1904.
Another account credits Khettranath Nag with inventing it earlier, during the reign of Maharaja Mahatabchand.

history.text: Bardhaman Mihidana became a Geographical Indication of West Bengal on 29 April 2017.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Shukto
summary: A gently bitter-sweet medley of vegetables such as bitter gourd, potato, sweet potato, raw banana and aubergine in a light milky sauce, eaten first in a Bengali meal.

history.text: Shukto is mentioned in medieval Bengali Mangal-Kavya poems and in biographies of Sri Chaitanya.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Beginning a meal with bitter foods is an old practice promoted by Ayurvedic writers.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

current_form_note: Today's shukto uses potato and sweet potato, so it can't be the same dish as the medieval one.

name: Litti chokha
summary: Wheat dough balls stuffed with spiced sattu (roasted gram flour), roasted over a fire, eaten with chokha, a smoky mash of aubergine, tomato and potato with mustard oil.

history.text: Litti is said to have been a staple of the armies of Magadha because it keeps well. Our source marks this claim as needing a citation.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: It is tied to religious events such as the Panchkosi yatra and the Lota-Bhanta mela around Buxar.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

current_form_note: Chokha with tomato and potato can't be older than those crops in India.

name: Silao khaja
summary: A flaky, many-layered pastry of wheat flour and khoya, deep-fried and soaked in syrup, from Silao near Nalanda. Often compared to baklava.

history.text: A folk tale says the Buddha was offered khaja at Silao while travelling from Rajgir to Nalanda.
history.label: TRADITIONAL

history.text: Archaeologist J. D. Beglar described the Silao sweet during his survey there in 1872–73 and linked it to King Vikramaditya.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: The GI Registry granted Silao Khaja a Geographical Indication in December 2018.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

name: Dhuska
summary: A deep-fried bread of ground rice and chana dal batter, puffed and golden, sold at market stalls across Jharkhand and eaten with chutney or curry.

history.text: Our source makes no claim about its origin or age.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Pitha (Assam)
summary: Rice-flour cakes made for Bihu: til pitha is rolled around roasted sesame and jaggery; ghila pitha is fried with jaggery. Often made from sticky bora rice.

history.text: In Assam, pitha is a special class of rice dishes made mainly for occasions such as Bihu.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Our source gives no origin story for Assamese pitha. A legend about the Buddha in the same article concerns an Odia pitha, not Assam's.
history.label: UNKNOWN

name: Chak-hao kheer
summary: A purple-black rice pudding made by slow-cooking Manipur's aromatic black rice, chak-hao, in milk with sugar.

history.text: Chak-hao black rice (not the kheer itself) received a Geographical Indication on 20 April 2020, after a producers' group from Imphal applied in 2017.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: The rice is used for ceremonies and special occasions.
history.label: DOCUMENTED

history.text: Our source gives no date for chak-hao kheer.
history.label: UNKNOWN
